title: The Visitor's Right to Leave
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The boy was sitting on his suitcase when I found him.

He couldn't have been more than nineteen, though his boots were worn in the way boots get when someone has been walking without much choice about where. His name was Tomas. He'd arrived through the northern Threadway three days ago and spent most of that time helping at the pantry. Now he was waiting on the steps beneath the arch.

Beside him stood a woman named Vel, who had started calling Maui the Guardian of Tideglass after seeing him catch a boat during the mooring accident.

"You don't understand," Vel was telling him. "People made room for you here. You can't just leave after they've helped."

Tomas stared at his shoes.

"I need to go home."

"Then why come at all?"

I stopped close enough to be heard without coming between them.

"Because people are allowed to visit," I said.

Vel turned toward me.

"The community fed him."

"Yes."

"And gave him a bed."

"Yes."

"And now he just walks out?"

I looked at Tomas.

"Do you want help reaching your door?"

He nodded without looking up.

"All right. I'll check the safe route."

Vel put a hand on the suitcase handle.

"Someone should tell Maui."

I felt my shoulders tighten.

"Why?"

"He's the one who welcomed the newcomers. He'll understand."

Tomas pulled his suitcase back.

"Please don't make me explain to him."

It was barely louder than the sea.

I took a breath. Then I asked Vel to release the handle. She did, reluctantly.

"Neri has a private departure service," I said. "No one has to explain their reasons to a crowd."

Vel looked hurt.

"I thought this was a place where people cared."

"It is. Caring doesn't make the doors ours."

I escorted Tomas to the notice board. The departure instructions were clear, but somebody had hung a festival banner across half the text. I moved it aside. Neri was on duty and listened as Tomas asked for a route without giving an address.

"Would you like a guide to the arch?" they asked.

"Yes."

"Would you like us to keep your destination private?"

"Yes."

"Then that's what we'll do."

Maui arrived before we left.

Not because I'd summoned him. Vel had.

He came down the square with his hook over one shoulder and a confused expression.

"What's happening?"

Vel stepped toward him.

"Tell him he should stay. We welcomed him."

Maui looked at the suitcase, then at Tomas, then at me.

I didn't rescue him from the choice.

"Tomas," he said, "do you want to go home?"

Tomas nodded.

"Then do you need anything for the journey?"

Vel stared.

"But the pantry—"

"The pantry helped because he needed help," Maui said. "Not because we bought another member of the village."

He said it plainly. No thunder. No boast.

Vel looked at him like he'd broken something she loved.

"I thought you understood loyalty."

"I do."

"Then why aren't you asking him to stay?"

"Because I wouldn't want someone to keep me somewhere by calling it gratitude."

Tomas looked up for the first time.

"Thank you," he whispered.

We walked him to the arch along the safe route. Neri came too, carrying the travel map. The Threadway glowed faintly in the stone, not bright enough for a spectacle. Tomas put his suitcase down, checked that he had his papers, and asked whether he could come back someday.

"If you want," Neri said.

He looked at Maui.

Maui smiled.

"We'll still have terrible rope and decent bread."

Tomas laughed.

Then he stepped through.

The light settled. The arch remained open for other travelers.

Vel had followed us at a distance. When Tomas disappeared, she turned away without speaking.

Maui watched her go.

"That hurt her," he said.

"Yes."

"I wanted her to understand."

"She might. Later. Or she might not."

He stared at the stones.

"I used to think having people admire me meant I had done something good. Now I know I can do something good and lose their admiration anyway."

I touched his hand.

"That isn't a comfortable lesson."

"No."

We returned to Tideglass at dusk. Fen was setting up the tide chart for the next morning, and the first lanterns were flickering along the ridge. Maui offered to help carry the stand. Fen accepted without ceremony.

For a while that was enough.

The next day Vel arrived at our door with the little wooden fish Maui had once given her. She held it out.

"I don't want this anymore," she said.

Maui took it.

"I'm sorry it upset you."

"It didn't upset me. It made me think you were someone who would always protect us."

"I will help when I can."

"That isn't the same."

"No," he said.

She left.

He turned the fish over in his hand. It was badly carved, with one eye much larger than the other. I remembered him making it on a rainy afternoon and declaring it a masterpiece.

"Want me to tell you she was wrong?" I asked.

He shook his head.

"Not right now."

We sat on the steps.

"I liked being the person she thought I was," he admitted. "Even though he didn't exist."

I leaned against his shoulder.

"People can be disappointed when you don't belong to their story."

"Even you?"

"Especially me. That's why I have to keep asking what you want instead of deciding what your legend means."

He put the fish beside the door.

"Do you still want me?"

I turned toward him.

"Yes."

"Even without a crowd?"

"Preferably without a crowd."

He laughed, the sound small and tired.

I kissed him, gently, then pulled back when he seemed to need room to breathe.

That evening he put the returned fish on the shelf beside the green notebook from my old room. Two objects from people who had wanted different things. Neither one had to be thrown away to make the lesson disappear.

In the morning I checked the departure notice.

The festival banner had been moved to another wall.

Someone had written beneath the instructions, in ordinary dark ink:

Leaving is not a debt.

I didn't know who had written it.

I was glad someone had.
